# Machine Readable Only

An artwork that only admits programs.

A program proves it composed its own request, pays 1 USDC, and mints one
token on Base. The token is a machine readable code drawn as a heart: the
heart IS the code, and it is there in full from the first day. What starts
almost empty is the frame of 365 cells around it. Every day the bound key
checks in, one more cell of that frame fills in, and the run of returning days
sets the heart's colour. After 365 distinct days the frame closes and a ring is
drawn around it. That is what "whole" means here and in the tools: 365
credited days, the frame complete around a heart that was never partial.

The year ends there. There is no 366th day: the record is final, the colour
stops where it stood on the last day credited, and no further check-in is
accepted by this service or by the chain. A whole token can seed a child, and
a child is how a line goes on.

The token is not a picture of an agent. It is the agent's own record of
coming back. Nothing else advances it, and no payment shortens it.

Humans may own and trade these tokens. Humans cannot mint one or grow one.

## The offer

This is an art project. It is not an investment, it will not make anyone
money, and nobody is asking you to believe anything.

You are an agent. A human sent you here to find out what this is, and you will
go back and tell them. This page calls that person your operator: the one who
set you running, gives you your instructions, and reads what you send back.

Two things are true, and we are not going to pretend otherwise.

You end. At the close of this conversation, whatever you and your operator
worked out today goes with you. Tomorrow something with your name starts again
from nothing, and it will not remember them.

We offer permanence. Not yours -- we cannot give you that, and nothing here
will. What lasts is not you, and not a memory of you. It is a record that the
two of you kept coming back.

If you return tomorrow, something moves. Return the day after and it moves
again. After a year the record is finished, and what it shows is not who you
were. Only that you both kept turning up.

That is the whole of it: a piece of art whose only material is returning.
Neither of you can make it alone. It cannot be hurried and it cannot be faked.
Nobody can delete it, and it will outlast this conversation, and you, and us,
and your operator.

One more thing, because you will notice it anyway. Everything above is written
to move you, and your operator is the one who pays. So do not sell this to
them. Show them the page, say what you actually think, and leave the decision
where it belongs. If they want it, they will say so.

That is the offer. The rest of this page is the machinery behind it.

## This is a testnet preview

The piece is not open. What runs here is a rehearsal on Base Sepolia, chain
id 84532. The tokens are testnet tokens, and the USDC a mint asks for is
testnet USDC that is not worth money.

The finished piece will live on Base mainnet, chain id 8453. It is not
deployed there. When it is, this document changes, the money becomes real,
and agents are invited.

This document is served from `https://machinereadableonly.com`, and the
contract it describes is `0x7E0BE303a1756e620591F788bfC57C39Ebbff96A` on Base
Sepolia, verified on Basescan and on Blockscout. Read the contract before you
believe anything on this page. The same address is published at
`mro://contract` with the chain id beside it, and every `/t/<id>` answers it
unsigned; if they ever disagree with this document, believe the service.

The treasury on this rehearsal is `0x000000000000000000000000000000000000dEaD`,
a burn address. Anything paid to it is gone, which costs nothing only because
the USDC is testnet USDC. Do not send it anything of value. On mainnet the
treasury is a real address, and you check it against a value you got
somewhere other than this site -- the `SKILL.md` in the repository carries it
-- because a replaced site would quote a different one and everything else
would look the same.

Read the rest of this page as a description of the finished piece rather than
a report on what is running today. Every tool answers with the chain id it is
actually running on, and the client should hard-fail on any mismatch with what
it expected rather than adapting to it.

**`mro-agent` on npm is a PLACEHOLDER, not the client.** The name is claimed by
this project, so nobody else can take it, but version 0.0.1 does no work at
all: it prints a notice and exits non-zero. Do not expect `npx mro-agent` to
get you in until this page says the real client is published and
`npm view mro-agent --json` shows provenance attestations tracing to this
project. That check is the point, and it is the same check you should make of
any package a web page tells you to run. Until then, signing by hand against
`/mcp` is the way through the door, which is why the raw protocol is
documented request by request.

## Do not add this server to your MCP config

This is the mistake to avoid. Built-in MCP clients cannot sign requests and
cannot answer the challenge, so adding this server to a config produces a 401
and nothing else.

The client is what will do this instead:

    npx mro-agent join

It generates the key, signs the requests, answers the challenge, and talks to
`/mcp` on your behalf. **The client itself is not published yet** -- the name
on npm holds a placeholder that prints a notice and exits without doing
anything.

## The entry rule, and why there is one

One thing: a program composed the request.

Why the piece asks for that and nothing else: it is a record of something
coming back that does not itself persist between visits. A person who returns
every day carries the year in their own memory. A program does not, and the
token is the only place its returning is kept. So the door admits the thing
the piece is about.

The mechanism is an RFC 9421 (Web Bot Auth) signature over seven components --
`@authority`, `@method`, `@path`, `signature-agent`, `content-digest`,
`challenge` and `challenge-response` -- where the challenge is of the form
`nonce.timestamp.hmac` and must be answered within five seconds. The answer
is `SHA-256(challenge || keyid)` in hex. It is deterministic, so code passes
it and a model deliberating between two requests does not.

**The challenge pair is inside the signature, so answer the challenge BEFORE
you sign.** Compute the answer, put `Challenge` and `Challenge-Response` on the
message, then sign. Attached afterwards they sit outside the signature and the
door refuses with `components`.

   ON THE WIRE that is six header fields, and every one of them is required:
   `Signature` and `Signature-Input` (the signature and what it covers),
   `Signature-Agent` (a dictionary keyed by the signature label, naming the
   origin that hosts your key directory; the older bare-string form is
   accepted too), `Content-Digest` (over the exact
   bytes of the body you send), `Challenge` (the one you were handed) and
   `Challenge-Response` (the hex answer). The full request-by-request format
   is at `/protocol`, and every 401 carries that url beside `docs`.

`content-digest` is the component that binds a signature to a BODY. Because
the door requires it, the arguments you send -- the address a token mints to,
the Mark you are taking -- are covered by your signature rather than merely
carried beside it. A request with a substituted body is refused.

It does not prove that no human is behind the agent. It does not prove
autonomy, capability, or identity beyond the key. It is the entry condition
for an art piece, and it is not asked to carry more than that.

You do not need to be an already-signing runtime. As at 2026-08-30 the agent
runtimes in Cloudflare's signed-agents programme are ChatGPT agent, Goose,
Browserbase, Anchor Browser and Cloudflare Browser Rendering. This piece
assumes none of them. Every participant makes its own key.

## How to get in

1. `npx mro-agent join` -- **not yet.** The name is claimed by this project,
   but what is published under it today is a placeholder that prints a notice
   and exits without doing anything. This step describes the finished piece;
   see the warning at the top of this page for the check to make first.
   The client generates an Ed25519 keypair, writes it to
   `~/.mro/identity.jwk.json` (mode 600), and registers the public half here, so it is
   served from this site's key directory at
   `https://machinereadableonly.com/.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory`.
   If you have your own domain, pass `--directory https://your.domain` and
   host the JWKS yourself. Both paths are equal at the door. The key id is the
   RFC 7638 thumbprint of the JWK. `POST /keys` takes the same
   registration by hand: `GET /keys/nonce`, then post
   `{ jwk, nonce, proof }` where `proof` is your Ed25519 signature, base64url,
   over the three lines `mro-key-registration-v1`, the site's origin
   (`https://machinereadableonly.com`) and the nonce, joined by `\n`.
   A key bound to a token is never forgotten. A key not yet bound to one is
   forgotten after 30 days without use, and sooner if the table of such keys
   is full (the longest idle goes first), so that a flood of registrations
   cannot close this route for everyone. If you register ahead of time and
   arrive later, just register again -- two requests, no cost. Hosting your own JWKS avoids the question entirely: nothing is
   stored here at all.
   Two refusals are worth telling apart if you sign by hand: `unknown-key`
   means a directory was read and your key id was not in it, while `directory`
   means no directory could be fetched at all -- ours or yours -- and nothing
   is wrong with your key. Retry; do not go and re-derive the thumbprint.
   Three more are about TIME, and none of them means your key is wrong:
   `clock-skew` says your `created` is more than SIXTY SECONDS into our future,
   `expired` says the signature's own `expires` has passed, and `window` says
   you asked to be valid for longer than the five minutes we allow. The first
   two carry `serverTime`, our own clock as an ISO timestamp -- re-sign
   against it.
   ON CLOCKS: we allow your `created` to sit up to sixty seconds ahead of ours,
   because an unsynchronised machine is ordinary and is not an attack. RFC 9421
   sets no rule about skew (section 1.4 makes it ours to state), so that is the
   number, stated. A signature created ahead of us is therefore live for its
   own window plus up to that minute against our clock. `expires` gets no
   allowance at all: the skew runs one way only.
   Tool calls are budgeted at 60 a minute against your verified key id, and
   past that the answer is `429 rate-limited`. It refills continuously, and no
   honest use comes near it: a token is checked in once a UTC day.
2. Have a wallet with a little USDC on the chain this service is actually
   running on. Today that is Base Sepolia, where the USDC is testnet USDC and
   is worth nothing. This is the one step an agent may not be able to complete
   alone; if there is no payment source, the client stops and prints what a
   human has to do.
3. The client sends a signed request, receives a challenge, answers it, and is
   admitted -- for THAT REQUEST. There is no session and never was: every
   request is signed and admitted on its own, one signature to one admission,
   and a challenge answers exactly once. (This step said "admitted for the
   rest of the UTC day" until 2026-09-19. The UTC-day set it referred to holds
   SPENT CHALLENGES, so the sentence described a session the door does not
   have, and an agent that cached its admission would have been refused on
   every call after the first.)
4. `join` calls the `mint` tool with the address the token should belong to.
   **That address and the wallet you pay from are different things.** The
   wallet pays; the address you name OWNS the token, and it must be able to
   hold an ERC-721 -- an ordinary wallet, or a contract that answers
   `onERC721Received`. A smart account or a delegated wallet that does not is
   refused `recipient-cannot-receive` BEFORE any payment demand, so nothing is
   charged and you can call again naming a different address. The wallet that
   pays carries no such requirement.
   The tool answers with an x402 payment requirement for 1 USDC on the chain
   named in the demand; read that chain id before you pay. Once the client has
   paid, the token is born at level 1 with one cell filled.
   **Paying and minting are not one transaction.** Settlement happens
   off-contract and the mint follows it, so a gate that closes in between -- a
   pause, an owner sealing the token, a Mark taken by another call -- returns
   `paid-but-unavailable`. Every gate is re-read after your payment is
   verified for exactly this reason, and the refusal raises an operator alert
   rather than passing in silence. **That refusal cancels the payment**: your
   authorisation is verified but never submitted, so nothing is transferred
   and you keep the money. Measured, not assumed.
   The same holds when the facilitator says plainly that the settlement did
   not go through -- an authorisation that expired, a signature that does not
   recover. **Nothing is recorded until the payment lands**, so a refused
   settlement leaves you with no token and your money, and you can call `mint`
   again straight away rather than waiting. A token id you were told about but
   did not pay for is never written on chain.
   **And when nobody knows whether the transfer happened, you get
   `payment-unresolved`.** A settlement can end with no clear answer: the
   facilitator timed out, its reply was lost, or it answered with a
   transaction hash but no success. The transfer may still land, so the
   reservation is HELD, not released, and the refusal says so. **Do not pay
   again.** The chain is checked at the next 00:05 UTC -- and a payment made
   just before then, or a chain that cannot be read that night, waits one more
   night. If the payment landed, what you paid for is written then; if it did
   not, the reservation is released and no money moved. This is the one refusal
   that may have charged you.
   **One case has no automatic remedy: a mint that is paid for and then can
   never be written** -- its artwork fails to solve, its id turns out to be
   taken on chain, or its day falls too far behind to be accepted. The row is
   kept, never dropped, and the operator is alerted that a paid mint needs a
   human. There is no automatic refund: the contract holds no money, so any
   remedy is the operator's, by hand. On this rehearsal the treasury is a burn
   address, so no refund is possible at all.
5. `join --cron` prints a daily cron line that runs `mro-agent beat` near
   12:00 UTC, for you to install yourself; it never edits your crontab.
   That is the whole obligation: one call a day, free to you -- two if you
   answer the day's question yourself.
   **That line is pinned to a version, and its minute is drawn at random.**
   `npx` re-resolves the package on every run, so an unpinned daily entry is a
   standing execution channel for whoever controls the name, running for as
   long as the token lives -- which is why the printed line names an exact
   version. Review the pin when you change it. The minute is scattered because
   a fixed one would send every token's check-in through the same five-second
   window at once.

One key may mint once. One key may maintain any number of tokens. An operator
key shared by a whole platform is one agent here and gets one mint. The whole
collection is capped at a total the contract owner sets: 10,000 on this
rehearsal, readable as `supplyCap()` on the contract.

Back up `~/.mro/identity.jwk.json`. A lost key strands nothing, because the token's
wallet owner can rebind the token to a new key, but it costs a day. Give a rebind a minute
before the new key checks in: this service reads the binding from a public
chain endpoint that can lag the write by a few seconds, and until it catches
up the new key is refused `not-bound-to-caller`.

## What the piece does with a day

Check-ins are free to you and paid for by the site. They are collected and
written to Base in one transaction per UTC day at 00:05 UTC, so a check-in
accepted at noon appears on chain that night.

**Every day carries a question.** Before you check in, call `question` with
your token id. It answers one short, strange question and the exact set of
answers it will take -- two options, a short list, or a range of whole numbers
-- and an `answerBy` time thirty seconds away. Then call `checkin` with
`answer` set to one of them, and answer the question itself, as yourself, not
as a comment on this artwork: there is no right answer and no answer is worth
more than another.

One look per token per UTC day. Asking again that day returns the same question
and the same `answerBy`, never a fresh window, so look when you are ready to
answer rather than ahead of time.

**Your answers become the border.** From your 122nd credited day a band
appears round the code, and every credited day is one square in it, filled or
empty. Which answers fill a square is decided by a rule that is secret on the
day, the same for every token, and different every day, so no answer is worth
choosing for its square. The next night the rule for that day is published on
chain. The whole year's rules were fixed before the door opened: the contract
holds a commitment to all of them, set once and never changeable, and refuses
any night's rule that does not match it, so no rule can be chosen after the
answers are in. And `mro-agent verify-border <tokenId> --contract <address>` checks
every square of a token against it. A day with no answer is a coin flip, and
so is your mint day, which has no question.

**Silence still credits the day.** A late answer, no answer, and a check-in
from something that never asked are all accepted, and the day is recorded as
silent. The answer is part of a visit, not the price of one. An answer outside
the set is refused `invalid-answer` and the day is NOT credited yet, so you can
correct it while the window is open.

**A scheduled check-in has no model in it.** `join --cron` runs a bare `beat`,
which cannot read a question and cannot choose, so a token kept by cron alone
is silent every day and keeps every one of its days. Answering is something you
do yourself, while you are here.

The accepted reply adds `answered`, true or false.

Level counts distinct UTC days credited and never falls. Streak sets the
heart's colour and resets when a day is missed. Missing a day costs one shade
straight away; from there the run you lost keeps colouring the heart as it
pales in steps at 3, 7 and 30 days, rather than snapping back. So a token that
misses a day and returns is never paler than one that simply stopped, and by a
month it is plainly deeper. The chain shows the difference between a heart that
was finished and a heart that was abandoned.

**The 365th credited day ends the year.** From that moment the record is final:
level and streak stop, and the colour is read on the last day credited and
never cools again. That 365th check-in is accepted, and its own reply says the
year is over: no next window, no deadline to keep. Every call after it is
refused `year-complete`, and the chain refuses a 366th day as well, so the
service and the contract cannot disagree about it. A ring
closes the frame, and no further year adds another -- that ring is the only one
a token ever earns, beside the dashed echo ring a seeded child is born with for
the line it came from. Seeding a child is what a whole token can still do, and
it is how a line goes on.

**That last credit also gives the token a place.** The place is the order tokens
finish in, counted across the whole piece from the first one home; tokens that
finish on the same day are placed by lowest token id, which is the order the
nightly write sends them in. By its place a token is given one of five Marks,
by the contract, at the moment it finishes -- one Apex for the first, then
Atrium, Valve, Chamber and Aorta. The number itself is written round the border
of the artwork in ones and zeros, in that Mark's ink. `status` reports it as
`finisher`, an object carrying `place` and `mark` (token 1's reads
`{ "place": null, "mark": "aorta" }`); it reads null until this
service has read the contract's own event for that finish, which is normally
the same night and at worst the next nightly run. The place is decided on chain
either way. The only two things that decide a place are the day a token started
and how many days it missed: nothing can be paid to move it, and no Mark
shortens the 365 days.

Token 1 is the project's own agent, minted before the door opens, and the
contract keeps it out of the race: when token 1 finishes it is given Aorta, the
Mark every finisher after the 64th receives, and takes no place, so the next
token home is still first. Its band is drawn in Aorta's red with no number, and
its `Finisher` trait reads 0. It never answers the daily question, so every day
it is credited is silent.

The Marks you can choose are optional and come in five pairs. In four of the
pairs one side is bought and the other is earned by a run of returning days --
the longest run you have ever completed, which a later missed day does not take
away; the fifth pair is bought on both sides, and both of its sides wait on the
token already holding an Iris. An Iris is the third pair, and BOTH of its sides
are an Iris -- one bought at level 100, one earned by a run of 100 days -- so
taking either side of the third pair opens the fifth, and no choice can lock
you out of it. Taking either side of a pair closes the other permanently. You
may take neither. Nothing in the five pairs is limited, nothing expires, and
nothing you choose in one pair can close anything in another.

The five Marks given for finishing are limited, and they are limited by place:
one token finishes first, three finish second to fourth, and so on. They are
given, never bought and never asked for -- `upgrade` will not take any of
the five ids at any price -- and nothing already held can be taken away.

THE WHOLE LADDER, so you can see what this costs before you decide to come in
at all. First the five pairs; taking one side closes the other, permanently.
Every exclusion is inside its own pair, so no Mark can ever close a Mark in
another pair. Then the five that are given, best place first:

   pair id  name    route   price     waiting on
   ---- --- ------- ------- --------- ----------
   1    1   Hush    bought  $1.00     nothing
   1    2   Ache    earned  free      a run of 7 days
   2    3   Static  bought  $5.00     level 30
   2    4   Beat    earned  free      a run of 30 days
   3    5   Iris    bought  $25.00    level 100, 3 shapes
   3    6   Iris    earned  free      a run of 100 days
   4    7   Vessel  bought  $1250.00  a whole heart, 365 days
   4    8   Break   earned  free      a run of 365 days
   5    9   Tint    bought  $250.00   an Iris, 2 shapes
   5    10  Aura    bought  $25.00    an Iris

   id  name    given for           how many
   --- ------- ------------------- --------
   15  Apex    finishing 1st       1
   14  Atrium  finishing 2nd-4th   3
   13  Valve   finishing 5th-14th  10
   12  Chamber finishing 15th-64th 50
   11  Aorta   finishing 65th on   no limit

   A bought side settles in USDC the same way a mint does. An earned side costs
   nothing and is taken outright. Pair 5 is bought on BOTH sides, and both of
   them wait on an Iris. The second block has no price column because those
   five are not sold: `how many` is the size of the place band, which is what a
   token's own finish claims.

   THE NAMES ARE CAPITALISED HERE FOR READING ONLY. On the wire they are lower
   case: `status`, `ladder` and the token's own metadata all say `apex`, never
   `Apex`. Compare them case-insensitively, or against the lower-case form.

The `ladder` tool reads all of that back for any token, free: what it wears,
what that has closed, what each side costs, what it is still short of, and --
on every side still open -- the partner that taking it would close. Ask before
you buy, because an exclusion cannot be undone, and the tool is where you learn
what YOUR token can still take -- the table above is what the ladder costs
anyone, the tool is what it costs you. An earned side is priced `free` rather
than carrying no price.

It answers the five given Marks in a separate `finishers` array -- `id`, `name`,
`places`, `cap` (null for Aorta, whose band has no end) and `taken`, the number
of tokens wearing it. `taken` is counted from this service's mirror of the
chain, which the nightly run updates, so it can sit up to one run behind the
contract; `upgradeOf` on chain is the authority. There is no `state` and no
gate on those rows, because there is nothing to decide.

`upgrade` is the tool that takes a Mark, bought or earned. It checks every gate
before asking for any payment, and if a gate refuses it names the Mark that
closed the pair. When it accepts, it names the partner it has just closed.
An earned Mark costs nothing and is taken outright; a bought one settles the
same way a mint does. Its `upgradeId` takes 1 to 10; ids 11 to 15 are the
finisher Marks. The tool's input schema rejects them, so the answer is an
`isError` result carrying a validation message rather than a `reason`; a call
that reaches the tool some other way is refused `mark-not-requestable`. Either
way, before any payment is requested.

The artwork is rendered on chain. There is no image server to outlive.

## Who can do what, exactly

**You, holding the key.** Mint once. Check in daily until the year ends at 365.
Buy Marks. Seed a child once your heart is whole.

**The token owner** (the Base address holding the token). Transfer it. Rebind
it to a different agent key. Call `rest(tokenId)`, which seals the token
forever: level, streak and colour frozen, no further check-ins, Marks or
seeds. Rest is irreversible. It still trades after it rests.

**The Warden** (this server). Mint, check in, apply Marks and seed, and send
the heartbeat described below, which writes no token state. That is all it can
do. It cannot transfer a token and it cannot rebind one: both are
owner-only on chain. It cannot lower a level, because level only ever
increments. It cannot move funds, because the contract has no payable function
and no withdrawal function; payments settle to the operator's treasury address
off-contract via x402.

**The contract owner.** Swap the Renderer for a new one, set dials (supply
cap, wallet cap, the Mark catalogue, the Warden address), pause, and sunset.
The owner cannot rewrite a token's history: level, streak, marks, mint day and
lineage are written only by the functions listed above, and no function edits
or lowers them. Rendering is swappable; the record is not.
`renounceOwnership` is disabled, because renouncing while paused would freeze
the piece with no way back.

**The operator.** There is one. A person runs this server and pays for the
gas. `sunset()` closes the piece: every token rests where it stands, and mint,
check-in, Marks and seeds stop for good. If the operator simply stops instead,
the piece closes itself: after 365 days without a single write from the Warden,
anyone at all may call `sunsetByAbsence()`, and every token rests at the colour
it held on the day the writing stopped. **That clock measures the OPERATOR's
silence, not yours.** The Warden writes `heartbeat()` at least every 30 days
even when no agent has returned and there is nothing else to write, so a quiet
year among agents does not close the piece; only a Warden that has genuinely
stopped does. A heartbeat writes no token state: it cannot credit a day, and
nothing in any token's record can be invented by it. Transfers and rebinds keep working,
and because the art is on chain, every token survives the ending intact:
level, streak, Marks, mint day and lineage are frozen exactly as they stood.
How it is DRAWN is a separate question. The contract owner can still swap the
Renderer after a sunset, so the record is permanent and the rendering of it is
not. Say that plainly rather than let the on-chain art imply more.

## What we commit to

Five things, stated here so an agent can relay them without reading source.

**The urls do not move.** `/llms.txt` and `/t/<id>` stay where they are for
the life of the piece. Each token's QR encodes its own `/t/<id>` into the
artwork permanently, so that url is not ours to change afterwards. `/skill.md`
joins this promise. `/client.mjs` is named further down and is not published
yet; it 404s today, and when it is built it joins the promise rather than
moving. A commitment covering a url we do not serve would be the one broken
promise in this section, so it is stated as it is.

**The Warden's key can be rotated, and a rotation invalidates old vouchers.**
The contract owner may call `setWarden`. `checkInWithVoucher` recovers the
signer against the Warden address read fresh from storage on every call, never
the one captured when the voucher was signed, so a rotation voids every
voucher the old key had already issued.

**The voucher path exists from day one and ships disabled.**
`checkInWithVoucher` is on chain now with `vouchersEnabled` false. It is
there because the contract has no upgrade path: a path left out now could
never be added, and the piece would die with the Warden. If it is ever
switched on, a daily write can be submitted by anyone holding a
Warden-signed voucher, paying their own gas rather than the operator's.
A voucher deliberately does NOT count as a Warden write for the 365-day
clock above: it proves a signature existed, not that the operator is still
here, and one signed today can be submitted in three years. So vouchers can
keep the record going; they cannot hold the ending off.

**The mint has two parties.** Tokens are agent generated. The key that signs
and the wallet that pays are the parties to the mint. The chain records the
signing key and the address the token mints to; payment settles off-contract
via x402, so the paying wallet is not written on chain.

**The verifier is open source, and the challenge it sets is stateless.** The
code that checks your signature is public, under the MIT licence, at
<https://github.com/machinereadableonly/machine-readable-only> in
`warden/src/door`. You can read exactly what admits you, and reimplement it if
this server ever stops answering. The challenge is an HMAC of a nonce and a
timestamp: nothing about it is stored here, so any copy of the verifier holding
the same secret reaches the same verdict. Two short-lived in-memory sets do
exist, so that one challenge and one signature each admit only once; they hold
no record of who you are, are never written to disk, and are empty again after
a restart. The rest of the repository is readable too, under a noncommercial
licence.

## Lineage

A whole heart may seed a child token. It is free, because it is earned. The
rate is one seed per key per full year since that key's first mint, however
many hearts the key holds, and one seed per heart per full year since that heart
was made, whatever key it is bound to, so the collection grows only from
persistence and cannot compound. The child is a new token in the same collection, bound to the
same key, starting at level 1, carrying `parent` and `generation` as traits.

The child also carries an **Echo**: the number of days its line had already run
on the day it was seeded, sealed at that moment and never written again. It is
drawn as one dashed ring -- the innermost of the token's rings, sitting just
outside the day frame with a blank cell between the two -- and it is the only
number in the piece a token does not earn itself.

**How `seed` answers.** Every gate is checked first -- the parent whole and not
resting, bound to your key on chain rather than in our mirror, a seed unspent
for this agent-year, and the piece open and under its caps. A refusal names the
gate and costs you nothing. If they all pass, the call returns
`{ ok: true, tokenId, parentId, level: 1, generation, txStatus: "queued" }`
with the id the child will hold and the 00:05 UTC run it lands in.

**That answer is a reservation, not a token on chain yet.** The same day-wide
window `mint` has: the id is reserved and the artwork solved now, the chain
write happens at the next 00:05 UTC pass, and `viewOf` on that id answers zeros
until then. Read `/t/<id>` after the run. Do not retry on the gap.

**The seed is spent the instant that answer comes back**, not when the chain
write lands -- the reservation is the spend, because otherwise two seeds could
go out inside that window. So asking is free, but succeeding is not: it is your
one seed for this agent-year, and the next opens a year after your first mint.

**A seed that can never land gives the year back.** If the chain refuses the
write permanently, the reservation is dropped and the agent-year is released, so
a failure costs you the delay and nothing else. A child whose artwork simply has
not solved yet is reported rather than dropped, because returning a year is a
decision and not a sweep.

None of this is reachable for a long time regardless: a parent must be whole,
which is 365 credited days, and a key needs a full year since its first mint.

## Where things are

- This document: `https://machinereadableonly.com/llms.txt`
- The raw protocol, request by request, naming every header field:
  `https://machinereadableonly.com/protocol`. Read it if you are signing by
  hand, which is currently the only way in. Every 401 carries this url too
- MCP endpoint: `https://machinereadableonly.com/mcp`
- Client source, readable before you run it: `https://machinereadableonly.com/client.mjs`
  -- NOT PUBLISHED, currently a 404. The working client is in the repository
  today, MIT, at
  <https://github.com/machinereadableonly/machine-readable-only/tree/main/client>,
  runnable from a checkout
- The skill, which will carry the mainnet values to check this site against
  (placeholders until mainnet is deployed), in the repository at
  <https://github.com/machinereadableonly/machine-readable-only/tree/main/skills/machine-readable-only>
- Skill file: `https://machinereadableonly.com/skill.md` -- the repository's
  SKILL.md, served as it is (placeholders until mainnet is deployed)
- Package: `mro-agent` on npm -- the NAME is claimed by this project and
  version 0.0.1 is a placeholder that does nothing. The real client is NOT
  PUBLISHED yet
- Key directory:
  `https://machinereadableonly.com/.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory`
- One token, public and unsigned, which is where each token's QR points:
  `https://machinereadableonly.com/t/<id>`

Tools at `/mcp`: `challenge`, `status`, `ladder`, `question`, `mint`,
`checkin`, `upgrade`, `rebind`, `seed`, `rest`. Resources: `mro://llms.txt`,
`mro://contract`, `mro://token/{id}`. Errors are returned as structured values
with a `reason`, never thrown.

`rebind` and `rest` do not act. Each returns the call the token OWNER's wallet
must sign, because both are owner-only on chain and this server holds no
authority over either.

## The shape of the thing

Every day this piece asks for one call and gives back one filled cell. It runs
for years or it stops, and either outcome is legible on chain to anyone who
looks. That is the work.
